newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa growth pessimism overdone - Syfrets.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa growth pessimism overdone - Syfrets.

text.p: Current pessimism about the South African economy was overdone and it should prove more resilient than expected, buoyed by an expected interest cut in the third quarter, Syfrets Ltd economist Sandra Gordon said on Friday.
In her latest economic review, Gordon said that structural changes in the economy and a still-favourable external environment would help underpin an overall growth rate of about two percent in 1997.

"We believe that current pessimism regarding the outlook for growth is somewhat overdone with forecasts for growth in both 1997 and 1998 being steadly downgraded and some suggestion of a recession," she said in her review.
"We are getting indications now that the second quarter figures will be quite strong and that there will be no recession," she told Reuters.
She forecast growth of three percent for 1998, but said that this did not factor in the possible disruptive effects of the El Nino weather phenomenon.

Although domestic demand was set to slow over the next 12 months, a rebound in consumer spending was expected in the second half of 1998 after a series of interest rate cuts, starting in the third quarter of this year.
Individual real income, which had been eroded by rising inflation last year, should recover during the rest of 1997 as inflation continued its downward trend.

Fixed investment spending was expected to remain relatively robust and would be less interest rate-sensitive than usual as government's ability to deliver improved and large budget roll-overs were finally spent.

"Furthermore, the continued process of privatisation should further boost investment spending by the parastatals while government initiated public-private partnerships (in infrastructure projects) should underpin private sector activity," she said.
Although increased export earnings had been limited so far this year, relatively robust international growth and the weakening of the rand should help boost export earnings over the next 18 months.
"Of particular interest is the strong performance visible in manufactured exports as weak local demand forces producers to shift their attention to potential export markets," Gordon said.

Imports were likely to continue to slow in line with weaker domestic spending with the main demand being for machinery and equipment for infrastructure projects and for renewed oil imports as strategic oil stockpiles were wound down.

Gordon said that the balance of payments constraint on growth had eased and there had been a limited reaction to the lifting of exchange controls. Although the outflow of individuals' funds was expected to pick up, "a stampede is certainly not expected."
She expected inflation to fall to around seven percent by the end of the year, bringing the average for the year to about 8.7 percent.
